questions.q: What is the key difference between modeling data as a team-level admin and modeling data as an enterprise architect, according to this lesson?
options: There is no real difference; the skills are identical at any scale
An architect designs for every team, system, and future requirement an object will ever touch, not just today's team's needs
Architects never use standard objects, only custom objects
Admins are not allowed to create relationships between objects
questions.explain: The lesson frames the shift as one of time horizon and blast radius: an architect has to design for the whole enterprise's current and future needs, not just one team's immediate requirement.

questions.q: Two business units in the same org each build their own 'Customer' object independently, and revenue reporting now requires reconciling two disagreeing systems. Which category of data-modeling cost does this illustrate?
options: A performance wall
A reporting cost
A governance gap
An integration failure
questions.explain: The lesson specifically describes this exact scenario as a reporting cost: reports that can't be trusted because no shared definition exists.

questions.q: A parent Account accumulates millions of child records under a single owner, slowing down sharing recalculation and search across the whole org. What is this an example of?
options: Data skew
Classification drift
A governance gap
A conceptual model
questions.explain: The lesson defines data skew as an imbalance in record distribution -- too many child records under one parent, or too many records under one owner -- that degrades performance at scale.

questions.q: Per the lesson, why are the failure modes of weak enterprise data modeling easy to miss at first?
options: Because Salesforce prevents all data modeling mistakes automatically
Because they rarely show up as an error message -- they show up later as untrustworthy reports, broken integrations, performance walls, or governance gaps
Because only Lesson 7 of this course covers failure modes
Because weak data models are always caught during initial testing
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly says these failure modes rarely show up as an error message, and instead surface later as compounding, predictable costs.

questions.q: Which lesson in this chapter is identified as covering one of the highest-consequence, hardest-to-reverse decisions on the platform?
options: Lesson 2, conceptual vs. logical vs. physical models
Lesson 5, data modeling patterns
Lesson 7, person accounts and contact models
Lesson 1, this lesson itself
questions.explain: The chapter overview specifically flags Lesson 7 (person accounts and contact models) as one of the highest-consequence, hardest-to-reverse decisions in the whole platform.
